To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

i) the NMSSM with {\lambda} close enough to unity and stop masses around 1 TeV is the most natural NMSS, i.e. the one with the lowest fine tuning of the Higgs mass; ii) the Higgs boson at 126 GeV can be accommodated in such an NMSSM, but the region of parameters that is compatible with all measurements is very small;
a most natural NMMSM is compatible with the Higgs measurements and that the production of a heavy Higgs scalar together with a lighter one is a very promising channel at the LHC to test the NMSSM.

the Higgs sector in the most natural NMSSMs is very similar to that of the MSSM, except that the Higgs couplings are somewhat different, and that the NMSSM is not in conflict with gauge coupling unifcation, but in fact can be a solution to the gauge coupling hierarchy problem.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the most natural NMSSMs, a 126 GeV CP-even Higgs boson can be accompanied by a heavier one, and that the latter can be detected at the LHC.
a {\lambda} ~1 NMSSM with stop masses below 500 GeV is a very good candidate to be tested at the LHC and at future colliders.
the NMSSM can provide a natural explanation to the observed Higgs boson, but only if it is the lightest scalar in the Higgs system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a light stop and a light Higgs singlet are not in conflict with the Higgs data.
a light Higgs singlet is a natural and unavoidable consequence of the most natural NMSSSM, and its discovery will be a clear signature for new physics at the TeV scale.
the NMSSM with {\lambda} ~1 and stop masses below ~ 1 TeV is a very attractive scenario, with a rich phenomenology and with the potential to explain all the Higgs data.
